title: Reinforcement Learning via Fixed-point Flow Matching

paper.title: Reinforcement Learning via Fixed-point Flow Matching
paper.abstract: Abstract In maximum entropy and behavior-constrained reinforcement learning (RL), the optimal policy is given by a Boltzmann distribution. Generating samples from this distribution can be challenging, as it is often complex and multimodal. While flow policies trained with flow matching provide a powerful framework for representing such distributions, they traditionally rely on access to training data, which is generally unavailable in online RL. To address this limitation, we propose fixed-point flow matching (FFM), a data-free procedure for training and fine-tuning flow policies in RL. FFM leverages the target flow identity to formulate the actor update as a fixed-point iteration, utilizing a flow-matching-style regression objective where the critic’s action gradients serve as regression targets. We show that the optimal policy is a fixed point of this iteration. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that FFM effectively fine-tunes pretrained flow policies in the offline-to-online setting and enables efficient and accurate training of flow policies from scratch in online RL. These results establish fixed-point flow matching as a principled approach for learning expressive flow-based policies without requiring training data.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
Across a range of reinforcement learning (RL) formulations, the improved policy is available in closed form as a Boltzmann distribution of the current critic. In maximum entropy RL, π ⋆ ​ ( x ∣ s ) ∝ exp ⁡ ( Q ⁡ ( s , x ) / λ ) \pi^{\star}(x\mid s)\propto\exp(Q(s,x)/\lambda) is optimal for the policy improvement step of soft policy iteration ( Ziebart et al., 2008 ; Haarnoja et al., 2017 ; Haarnoja et al., 2018 ) ; in KL-regularized and behavior-constrained RL, which includes offline-to-online fine-tuning, the same expression appears tilted by a reference policy ( Peters et al., 2010 ; Abdolmaleki et al., 2018 ; Peng et al., 2019 ; Nair et al., 2020 ) . This target distribution can be complex and multimodal whenever several distinct action choices are viable, but the classical actor–critic recipe projects it onto a Gaussian due to the simplicity of the resulting optimization problem and the tractability of the policy’s log-likelihood ( Haarnoja et al., 2018 ) . Flow and diffusion models ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) remove this representational restriction and have become the policy class of choice wherever a dataset is available ( Chi et al., 2023 ; Reuss et al., 2023 ; Janner et al., 2022 ; Park et al., 2025b ) . Yet, the stable training objectives that are used to train these models are not directly usable for online RL due to a lack of samples from π ⋆ \pi^{\star} . Existing methods for training flow and diffusion models in the on-policy RL setting often require backpropagating the critic through the integrator ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Ding & Jin, 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Celik et al., 2025 ; Le et al., 2026 ) , whose memory cost grows with every integration step and quickly becomes prohibitive, or rely on importance-weighted regression ( Ding et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2025 ) , whose exponential critic weights have high variance and lead to unstable training updates. Moreover, methods for fine-tuning flow models typically use stochastic optimal control, which requires converting the flow into a diffusion model in order to use the adjoint method ( Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025 ; Li & Levine, 2026 ; Dong et al., 2026b ) . In this work we ask whether a flow policy can be trained against a Boltzmann target with the same simple regression that makes flow matching stable, but without samples from the target. It replaces the data-derived regression target of flow matching by a critic-derived one, and the resulting objective, target flow matching , has the same minimizer as flow matching while reading its targets off the critic instead of a dataset. Since the objective still averages over samples of the target, we evaluate it with samples of the current policy and iterate. The resulting fixed-point flow matching (FFM) update, illustrated in Figure 1 , generates actions with the current flow, labels them with critic gradients, noises them, and regresses the velocity field onto the labels. We show that the optimal policy is a fixed point of this iteration. The whole procedure is conceptually simple, easy to implement and requires neither backpropagation through the integrator nor importance weights or conversion into a diffusion model.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: • The target flow identity and target flow matching ( Section 4 ). We derive an identity that expresses the velocity field of a Boltzmann target as a conditional expectation of the gradient of its log-density, and turn it into target flow matching, an alternative training objective to flow matching that shares its population minimizer but regresses onto the gradient of the target rather than onto the displacement of the data. • Fixed-point flow matching ( Section 4 ). We propose a fixed-point iteration that evaluates the target flow matching objective with samples of the current policy instead of the optimal one, and prove that the optimal policy is a fixed point of this iteration (Theorem 3 ). • Extensions ( Section 5 ). We further introduce several extensions for flow policies: a trust-region loss in velocity space, a loss for behavior-constrained fine-tuning that reads the reference score off the pretrained flow, and correlated exploration through temporally correlated prior draws. • Two RL instantiations ( Section 5 ). We instantiate FFM for maximum entropy RL and for offline-to-online fine-tuning. We validate both across 50 50 offline-to-online tasks and 24 24 online tasks ( Section 6 ), where FFM is competitive with or better than the strongest available baselines.

sections.heading: Reinforcement learning with diffusion and flow policies.
sections.text: Diffusion and flow models entered RL through imitation learning and offline RL, where a dataset makes their standard training objectives applicable and the critic enters through weighting, guidance, or gradients through the sampling chain ( Janner et al., 2022 ; Chi et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ; Lu et al., 2023 ; Kang et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Ding & Jin, 2024 ; Park et al., 2025b ) . In online RL there are no samples of the target policy, and existing methods differ in how the critic drives the actor update. One line backpropagates the critic value through the sampling chain ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Ding & Jin, 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) , which is memory-intensive and unstable for many integration steps. A second line uses critic-weighted regression, interpreting the denoising loss as a variational bound or as a mirror-descent step ( Ding et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2025 ) , and a third estimates policy gradients through the denoising process, typically under a trust region ( Ren et al., 2025 ; McAllister et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ; Le et al., 2026 ; Lv et al., 2026 ) . Closest to FFM are methods that use the action gradient of the critic: DIPO ( Yang et al., 2023 ) clones actions improved by gradient ascent on Q Q ; QSM ( Psenka et al., 2024 ) regresses the score onto ∇ x Q \nabla_{x}Q evaluated at the noisy action, a plug-in approximation of the target score identity that is exact only at the clean end; and RFM ( Li et al., 2026 ) estimates the exact posterior-mean target by self-normalized importance sampling, using Langevin–Stein control variates to interpolate between Q Q -weighted noise averages and Q Q -weighted averages of ∇ x Q \nabla_{x}Q , which allows it to train flow policies as well. Maximum entropy RL with generative policies additionally requires an entropy estimate: DACER ( Wang et al., 2024 ) fits a Gaussian mixture, DIME ( Celik et al., 2025 ) and MaxEntDP ( Dong et al., 2025 ) use a lower bound and numerical integration, respectively, Sanokowski & Patil (2025) augment the MDP with the denoising steps, FLAG ( Kim et al., 2026 ) uses importance sampling in the latent space of the flow, and AMDP ( Thilges et al., 2026 ) amortizes the entropy-regularized update with adjoint matching. FFM obtains the entropy from the divergence of the velocity field it trains, using the instantaneous change of variables.

sections.heading: Fine-tuning and offline-to-online RL.
sections.text: Reward fine-tuning of pretrained diffusion and flow models has been cast as policy gradient over the denoising chain ( Fan et al., 2023 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025b ) and as entropy-regularized stochastic optimal control ( Uehara et al., 2024 ; Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025 ) , with the KL divergence to the pretrained model as regularizer; Uehara et al. (2025) review the corresponding inference-time methods. The same behavior-tilted target governs offline-to-online RL with flow policies. FQL ( Park et al., 2025b ) distills the flow into a one-step policy that is trained by reparameterized critic gradients, DSRL ( Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ) keeps the flow fixed and learns a policy over its latent noise, ReinFlow and FINO ( Zhang et al., 2025a ; Shin et al., 2026b ) inject noise into the flow to obtain tractable likelihoods and exploration, and Q-Flow ( Doo et al., 2026 ) propagates terminal values to intermediate states of the flow. QAM ( Li & Levine, 2026 ) imports adjoint matching: the pretrained flow is converted into a memoryless SDE and critic gradients are transported backward along sampled trajectories by the lean adjoint ODE, and TRQAM ( Dong et al., 2026b ) stabilizes it with a path-space trust region. Concurrent work regresses velocity corrections onto critic gradients ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Ziakas et al., 2026 ) or steers a fixed flow policy at test time ( Zhou et al., 2026 ; Ruan et al., 2026 ) . FFM fine-tunes the pretrained flow directly in velocity space, requires neither SDE conversion nor adjoint simulation, and its behavior-tilted target has the KL-regularized optimum as a fixed point ( Appendix E ). Beyond the RL literature, FFM shares the fixed-point structure of the matching objectives used to train diffusion and flow models from unnormalized densities, and of adjoint matching; Appendix C discusses these methods, together with further critic-driven policy updates.

sections.text: We consider a Markov decision process with states s ∈ 𝒮 s\in\mathcal{S} , continuous actions x ∈ 𝒜 ⊆ ℝ d x\in\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} , transitions P ⁡ ( s ′ ∣ s , x ) P(s^{\prime}\mid s,x) , reward r ⁡ ( s , x ) r(s,x) , and discount γ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ) \gamma\in[0,1) . The state-action value function of the current policy π \pi is the expected discounted return Q π ( s , x ) = 𝔼 π [ ∑ k ≥ 0 γ k r ( s k , x k ) ∣ s 0 = s , x 0 = x ] Q^{\pi}(s,x)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\big[\sum_{k\geq 0}\gamma^{k}r(s_{k},x_{k})\mid s_{0}=s,\,x_{0}=x\big] when taking action x x in state s s and following π \pi thereafter. sections.heading: Offline-to-online RL.
sections.text: In offline-to-online RL, one commonly pre-trains a flow policy v ref v_{\mathrm{ref}} by flow matching Equation 6 and a critic by an offline method on a fixed dataset. The policy is then fine-tuned online, where it must stay close to the pretrained flow while it improves, since offline critics are reliable only near the data. This motivates the behavior-constrained objective of Section 3 . Prior work for fine-tuning flow policies typically converts the flow to a diffusion model with a specific (memoryless) noise schedule and leverages stochastic optimal control to compute adjoint states, which yield a stable regression objective for training ( Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025 ; Li & Levine, 2026 ; Dong et al., 2026b ) . sections.heading: Correlated exploration.
sections.text: A flow policy is a deterministic function of its prior draw, and hence, integrating Equation 5 from X 0 = σ 0 ​ ε X_{0}=\sigma_{0}\varepsilon yields the action x = Ψ θ ​ ( ε ∣ s ) x=\Psi_{\theta}(\varepsilon\mid s) , whose only source of randomness is ε ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( ⋅ , 0 , I ) \varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(\cdot;\,0,\,I\right) . Here, Ψ θ ( ⋅ ∣ s ) \Psi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s) is simply the sampler of the flow policy: the map that takes a prior draw ε \varepsilon and returns the clean action obtained by integrating the ODE with the learned velocity field. Hence, exploration can also be shaped by correlating the prior draws across environment steps. Similar to colored-noise exploration for Gaussian policies ( Eberhard et al., 2023 ) , we draw the priors within an episode from a stationary Ornstein–Uhlenbeck chain with correlation time τ ou \tau_{\mathrm{ou}} , i.e., ε k + 1 = e − 1 / τ ou ε k + 1 − e − 2 / τ ou ξ k , ξ k ∼ 𝒩 ( ⋅ ; 0 , I ) , ε 0 ∼ 𝒩 ( ⋅ ; 0 , I ) , \varepsilon_{k+1}\;=\;e^{-1/\tau_{\mathrm{ou}}}\,\varepsilon_{k}\;+\;\sqrt{1-e^{-2/\tau_{\mathrm{ou}}}}\;\xi_{k},\qquad\xi_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(\cdot;\,0,\,I\right),\qquad\varepsilon_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(\cdot;\,0,\,I\right), (20) and execute x k = Ψ θ ​ ( ε k ∣ s k ) x_{k}=\Psi_{\theta}(\varepsilon_{k}\mid s_{k}) . Therefore, the FFM regression Equation 11 , the entropy estimate Equation 15 , and the soft Bellman backup Equation 42 are unchanged, and so is the fixed point π ⋆ \pi^{\star} of Theorem 3 ; only the states the agent visits change. Instead of resampling the prior at every step, the agent commits to a direction for roughly τ ou \tau_{\mathrm{ou}} steps, which produces the sustained, directed behavior that sparse-reward tasks require before any reward is observed. We use it only for the hard-exploration tasks of Section D.4 . Other colored noise processes, such as the pink noise of Eberhard et al. (2023) , can be used as well, which we leave to future work.

sections.heading: 6 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate FFM in two settings: offline-to-online fine-tuning, and online on-policy maximum entropy RL, where we train a flow policy from scratch. For the offline-to-online setting, we focus on the ten OGBench ( Park et al., 2025a ) locomotion and manipulation domains totaling 50 tasks. For the online RL setting, we consider the GPU-accelerated MJX ( Zakka et al., 2025 ) Playground and humanoid tasks, which result in 24 tasks in total. We restrict ourselves to presenting the main results in this section, and refer the reader to Appendix E and to Appendix D for additional results and ablations, such as varying the number of integration steps, the interpolation schedules, or different trust region constraints.

sections.heading: Offline-to-online RL.
sections.text: We pretrain a behavior-cloning flow policy and a critic offline (to 1 1 M gradient steps) and then fine-tune online (to 1.5 1.5 M), against TRQAM ( Dong et al., 2026b ) , QAM (+QAM-E) ( Li & Levine, 2026 ) , FQL (+IFQL) ( Park et al., 2025b ) , DSRL ( Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ) , and CGQL-L ( Dong et al., 2026b ) under an identical protocol ( Figure 2 ). sections.heading: Online RL.
sections.text: We additionally train FFM in the online on-policy RL setting where the policy is trained from scratch. Concretely, we train FFM on the 20 MuJoCo Playground DMC ( Zakka et al., 2025 ) tasks and on the four MuJoCo Playground humanoid tasks that require precise high-dimensional control. We compare FFM’s performance against state-of-the-art Gaussian policy representations (REPPO ( Voelcker et al., 2026 ) , PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) , SPO ( Xie et al., 2025 ) ), diffusion policy representations (TRUDI ( Le et al., 2026 ) , AMDP ( Thilges et al., 2026 ) , DIME ( Celik et al., 2025 ) , DPPO ( Ren et al., 2025 ) ) and flow policy representations (FPO ( McAllister et al., 2026 ) ). Following Agarwal et al. (2021) , every learning curve represents the aggregated interquartile mean (IQM) with 95 % 95\% confidence intervals from a stratified bootstrap for every task in Figure 4 for the Playground tasks and in Figure 5 for the humanoid tasks, where every task is run on 10 10 seeds. While FFM performs comparably on the lower-dimensional Playground tasks ( Figure 3 left two panels and Figure 4 ), FFM converges faster to the highest performance alongside TRUDI on the more sophisticated, high-dimensional humanoid tasks. This indicates that FFM’s benefits are most visible in high-dimensional tasks. We further integrated correlated exploration into FFM and ran experiments on the Playground tasks. The resulting learning curves are shown in Figure 3 left two panels and Figure 4 for the aggregated and per-task results, respectively. Please note that we have run these experiments only on a subset of the tasks (see Figure 4 ). The aggregated FFM + OU curve (dashed in Figure 3 ) uses the FFM + OU learning curve on each task where we ran correlated exploration and the FFM learning curve on all other tasks. FFM + OU shows a faster convergence to a similar return value as the highest-performing baseline DIME, indicating that if computational resources permit, FFM’s performance can be boosted even more by tuning τ ou \tau_{\mathrm{ou}} . We have evaluated all methods on 10 10 seeds for every single environment (see Figure 4 and Figure 5 for results) and report the IQM with 95 % 95\% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals following Agarwal et al. This result indicates that FFM’s benefits are most pronounced on high-dimensional tasks. Furthermore, we can boost FFM’s performance by leveraging its deterministic mapping properties and incorporating correlated exploration (FFM + OU), which leads to a significantly faster convergence to a similar return value as the best-performing baseline DIME (left two panels) (see Figure 15 ).

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced fixed-point flow matching, a data-free procedure for training flow policies using a flow-matching-style regression objective. Its basis is the target flow identity, which expresses the velocity field as a conditional average of Q Q -scores at clean actions and thereby replaces the data-derived targets of flow matching by critic gradients. Evaluating the resulting objective on samples from the current policy instead of the optimal policy yields a fixed-point iteration that has the optimal policy as a fixed point. The construction is conceptually simple, easy to implement, and needs no gradients through the sampling chain, no conversion of the flow into a stochastic differential equation, and no adjoint simulation. We consider two instantiations of the proposed framework: an online maximum entropy actor–critic algorithm, and offline-to-online fine-tuning against a behavior-tilted target. Across 50 50 offline-to-online tasks and 24 24 online tasks, both are competitive with or better than the strongest available baselines.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: FFM requires a differentiable target. The regression target is built from the Q Q -score ∇ x Q ​ ( s , x ) \nabla_{x}Q(s,x) , so the critic must be differentiable in the action and the policy update is only as accurate as the critic’s gradient. This restricts FFM to continuous action spaces. Extensions to non-differentiable targets and discrete action spaces are left for future work.

sections.heading: Appendix C Extended related work
sections.text: This appendix complements Section 2 . The first paragraph places FFM in the family of matching objectives that train diffusion and flow models from an unnormalized target rather than from samples, which is where its fixed-point structure comes from. The second collects work on critic-driven updates of diffusion and flow policies that Section 2 groups but has no room to discuss individually.

sections.heading: Fixed-point methods for diffusion and flow models.
sections.text: Training a diffusion or flow model from an unnormalized density instead of samples is the problem of neural samplers. Early approaches minimize a path-space divergence by simulating the generative process ( Zhang & Chen, 2022 ; Vargas et al., 2023 ) . Matching-based samplers instead regress onto a target computed from the energy and its gradient: iDEM ( Akhound-Sadegh et al., 2024 ) , iEFM ( Woo & Ahn, 2024 ) , BNEM ( OuYang et al., 2026 ) , and EWFM ( Dern et al., 2025 ) estimate the noised score, velocity, or energy by importance-weighted Monte Carlo, target score matching ( De Bortoli et al., 2024 ) , on which FFM builds, writes the noised score as a conditional expectation of the clean-data score but requires samples of the target, and tilt matching ( Potaptchik et al., 2025 ) matches the velocity of a reward-tilted interpolant without reward gradients. These methods are iterative: the target is evaluated with samples of the current model and the regression is repeated, which is the fixed-point structure that Theorem 3 makes explicit for critic-driven targets. Adjoint matching ( Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025 ) forms a second family of such regressions. Proposed for reward fine-tuning, it has since been used for sampling from unnormalized densities ( Havens et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025a ; Mosso et al., 2026 ) , for discrete generative models ( So et al., 2026 ) , for faster fine-tuning pipelines ( Guo et al., 2026 ; Shin et al., 2026a ) , and in RL for policy extraction ( Li & Levine, 2026 ; Dong et al., 2026b ; Ghanem & Ghogho, 2026 ) and maximum entropy RL ( Thilges et al., 2026 ) ; its theory has been connected to the stochastic maximum principle ( Domingo-Enrich & Han, 2026 ) and unified with sampling ( Domingo-Enrich et al., 2026 ) . The bridge matching sampler ( Blessing et al., 2026 ) shows that these matching objectives, including adjoint sampling and ASBS, are fixed-point iterations rooted in Nelson’s relation and stabilizes them by damping. FFM belongs to this family with two differences: the target flow identity provides the regression target from critic gradients at clean actions, so no adjoint ODE is needed, and the target itself moves as the critic is learned.

sections.heading: Further critic-driven policy updates.
sections.text: Sorted by how the critic enters the actor update, the methods of Section 2 fall into a few families, and we record here the entries the main text omits. Methods based on backpropagation through time differentiate the critic through the entire sampling chain: besides those cited in Section 2 , Lv et al. (2025) constrain the update relative to a behavior policy. GenPO ( Ding et al., 2025 ) instead applies a PPO-style objective ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) to a diffusion policy whose likelihood is made tractable by a coupling construction. A second family avoids the chain by regressing onto improved actions : DIPO ( Yang et al., 2023 ) and Li et al. (2024) improve the actions stored in the replay buffer by gradient ascent on Q Q and then clone them with the standard denoising loss. This is the closest relative of FFM among the action-target methods, and the difference is that its regression target is an action rather than a velocity, so the noise level of the interpolant is not accounted for. A third family leaves the denoising loss in place and weights it by the exponentiated critic value ( Ding et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2025 ) , of which one-step flow policy mirror descent ( Chen et al., 2025 ) is the one-step variant, and flow map policies trained by mirror descent ( Dong et al., 2026a ; Gao et al., 2026 ) are the multimodal ones. None of these families obtains its target from the velocity field of the Boltzmann policy itself, which is what the target flow identity provides.

sections.heading: Environments and tasks.
sections.text: In our online on-policy RL experiments from Section 6 we have evaluated FFM on the GPU-accelerated MuJoCo Playground ( Zakka et al., 2025 ) tasks. More concretely, we distinguish between the 20 DeepMind Control (DMC) tasks of the suite, whose episode returns are bounded between [ 0 , 1000 ] [0,1000] , and the four MJX humanoid joystick tasks, which require precise and high-dimensional whole-body control and whose returns are not normalized. For every learning curve, we follow Agarwal et al. (2021) and report the interquartile mean (IQM) of the return with stratified bootstrapped 95 % 95\% confidence intervals over 10 seeds per task. Furthermore, in Figure 3 the aggregated results over all tasks for the Playground and the Humanoid tasks are reported, where the per-task results are shown in Section D.4 .

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare against Gaussian-policy methods, REPPO ( Voelcker et al., 2026 ) , PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) , and SPO ( Xie et al., 2025 ) , diffusion-policy methods, TRUDI ( Le et al., 2026 ) , AMDP ( Thilges et al., 2026 ) , DIME ( Celik et al., 2025 ) , and DPPO ( Ren et al., 2025 ) , and the flow-policy method FPO ( McAllister et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: D.4 Further experiments and design ablations
sections.text: Figure 4 and Figure 5 show the per-task learning curves on the 20 DMC tasks and the four humanoid tasks, respectively. An aggregation over all environments can be found in Figure 3 .

sections.heading: Interpolant schedule.
sections.text: As detailed in Section D.3 , we use a geometric interpolant schedule for the on-policy RL setting. We refer to Section D.3 for the exact parameter setting. A valid and intuitive interpolant is the linear schedule as described in Section 3 . However, the schedule type’s effect on performance is unclear, which is why we have conducted thorough experiments and report the aggregated results over the 20 Playground tasks together with their final performances and the Humanoid tasks together with their final performances in Figure 6 . In Figure 7 , we report the per-task results of the Playground suite, and the per-task results on the humanoid environments are shown in Figure 8 . While there seems to be only a minor, negligible difference in the aggregated results for the Playground tasks ( Figure 6 (left)), a clear difference can be seen in favor of the geometric schedule in the aggregated results for the humanoid tasks ( Figure 6 (right)). However, our experiments show that both schedules lead to a reasonably well-performing policy on average. Figure 6: Ablation. Geometric versus linear interpolant schedule. As discussed in Section D.4 , FFM is not restricted to a specific interpolation schedule type such as the linear schedule. Motivated by diffusion-based methods, we have compared the performance of a linear schedule to the geometric schedule as described in Section D.4 and report the aggregated results over all 20 MJX Playground tasks (left two panels) and the four humanoid tasks (right two panels), where every single task was run on 10 10 seeds, and we report the IQM and the stratified bootstrapped 95 % 95\% confidence intervals ( Agarwal et al., 2021 ) . While the results indicate that there is barely a performance difference in the Playground tasks, a slight improvement on the humanoid tasks can be seen, which is why we have chosen the geometric schedule as default for the online RL tasks. See Figure 7 and Figure 8 for the per-task results. Figure 7: Ablation. Geometric versus linear interpolant schedule (MJX Playground). We plot the IQM per-task learning curves with 95 % 95\% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals ( Agarwal et al., 2021 ) over 10 10 seeds on the 20 MJX Playground tasks. The performance between the schedule types is the same for most tasks and differs only for some tasks such as FingerSpin or PendulumSwingup , which, however, lie within the confidence intervals. Therefore, there is no statistically clear result on which interpolant should be used for the Playground tasks. Figure 8: Ablation. Geometric versus linear interpolant schedule (MJX Humanoid). We plot the IQM per-task learning curves with 95 % 95\% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals ( Agarwal et al., 2021 ) over 10 10 seeds on the four MJX humanoid tasks. While for the G1JoystickFlatTerrain and for the G1JoystickRoughTerrain tasks there is no difference in performance, it seems that the geometric schedule performs slightly better on the T1 tasks, which is why we have chosen the geometric schedule as default for the online RL experiments.

sections.heading: Number of integration steps.
sections.text: We further analyze the effect of the number of integration steps on the humanoid tasks’ performance. Figure 9 (left) shows the results aggregated over the four MJX humanoid tasks for different numbers of Euler integration steps K K . Please note that we only vary K K and keep everything else as detailed in Table 1 . The corresponding per-task curves to the aggregated results are shown in Figure 10 . As expected, the performance increases with the number of integration steps, since the integration error of the flow decreases. However, we observe that performance plateaus at K = 16 K=16 , where increasing to K = 32 K=32 does not improve performance and yields similar results. Based on this observation and the baseline’s hyperparameters, we use K = 16 K=16 throughout the paper for a fair comparison against the other diffusion- and flow-based methods ( Table 1 ). Figure 9: Ablation. Number of Integration Steps (left two panels) and Action Squashing mapping (right two panels). Number of integration steps (left two panels): We analyze the effect of varying integration steps and report the aggregated results over all four humanoid tasks (left two panels). Every single task was run on 10 10 seeds, and we report the IQM and the 95 % 95\% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals ( Agarwal et al., 2021 ) . The results indicate that with an increasing number of integration steps, the performance increases until it plateaus from K = 16 K=16 onwards, which is why we have chosen K = 16 K=16 as default in our experiments. Please see Figure 10 for the per-task learning curves. We have run experiments on the four MJX humanoid tasks and report the aggregated IQM with 95 % 95\% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals ( 10 10 seeds per task) ( Agarwal et al., 2021 ) in the two right panels. sections.heading: Action squashing.
sections.text: A key factor for stable training in actor-critic-based RL is that the generated actions need to be squashed to a valid region to avoid querying the critic at unreasonable action regions during the policy update. As detailed in Appendix D , there are two distinctive choices for the squashing function, namely, the tanh \mathrm{tanh} and the erf \mathrm{erf} functions. To assess the effect on the performance of the design choices, we have run FFM with a tanh \mathrm{tanh} squashing function while keeping all other design choices the same and report the aggregated learning curves on the humanoid tasks in Figure 9 (right), together with the final returns. The per-task results are shown in Figure 11 . sections.heading: Deterministic evaluation.
sections.text: During our experiments, we observed that starting the flow’s integration always at the central point X 0 = 0 X_{0}=0 during evaluation only, yields improved performance against the standard case, where X 0 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) X_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) is drawn from a standard normal distribution as done during training. This observation is depicted in Figure 12 , where we plot the aggregated learning curves on the Playground tasks together with their final returns (left) and the aggregated learning curves on the humanoid tasks together with their final returns (right). The per-task learning curves are shown in Figure 13 and Figure 14 respectively. While the improvement is not very obvious for the Playground tasks ( Figure 12 (left)), a clear and significant performance boost in the humanoid tasks can be observed ( Figure 12 (right)). This result indicates that, for high-dimensional tasks in particular, removing the stochasticity from the action generation process yields improved performance. While this observation is very interesting and worth a more detailed analysis, in particular from a theoretical point of view, we leave this analysis for future work and apply the deterministic evaluation throughout our experiments. sections.heading: Correlated exploration.
sections.text: A flow policy’s key benefit is that the action generation process is a deterministic mapping up to the sampling of the starting sample. As discussed in Section 5 , this allows us to apply a correlated exploration scheme, where the exploration is shaped by correlating the prior draws across the environment steps. To analyze the additional hyperparameter τ ou \tau_{\mathrm{ou}} that is introduced by Equation 20 , we have conducted experiments on single Playground tasks, where the initial instantiation of FFM, i.e., without correlated exploration, performs unsatisfactorily (see Figure 4 ). Figure 15 shows the learning curves on a subset of tasks that we have picked from the task suite to analyze the effect on performance for varying τ ou \tau_{\mathrm{ou}} values. We can observe that for each task, there exists at least one τ ou \tau_{\mathrm{ou}} value that outperforms the initial case without correlated exploration, and only for the FingerSpin and WalkerRun tasks, we observe that a too-high value yields decreased performance. Especially for the AcrobotSwingupSparse, HopperHop and HopperStand tasks, correlated exploration yields a significant improvement over the case without correlated exploration. However, the results also indicate that there is no global value for τ ou \tau_{\mathrm{ou}} that performs best across every task, which makes tuning this hyperparameter difficult and is only possible if enough compute resources are available. Nevertheless, we believe that correlated exploration is a useful feature that FFM can leverage. Figure 15: Ablation. Correlated Exploration. On a subset of the MJX Playground tasks, we analyze the effect of correlated exploration by varying τ ou ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 } \tau_{\mathrm{ou}}\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32\} , where we have run every curve on 10 10 seeds and report the IQM with 95 % 95\% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals ( Agarwal et al., 2021 ) . Correlated exploration can significantly boost FFM’s performance for the right choice of τ ou \tau_{\mathrm{ou}} . For example, the HopperStand task is solved, while FFM without correlated exploration struggles on this task.

In offline-to-online RL a fixed dataset 𝒟 \mathcal{D} of transitions is available before any interaction. sections.text: We follow the protocol of TRQAM ( Dong et al., 2026b ) . sections.heading: The two regimes.
sections.text: The rows of Table 4 are two coordinated settings rather than four independent knobs. In the sparse-reward mazes the critic is smooth and ∇ x Q \nabla_{x}Q is small, so we amplify it with 1 / λ = 30 1/\lambda=30 . This only works if the Fisher scale is held fixed at ℐ ¯ = 1 \bar{\mathcal{I}}=1 : an adaptive normalizer estimates ‖ ∇ x Q / λ ‖ 2 \|\nabla_{x}Q/\lambda\|^{2} and divides the amplification back out. In manipulation the chunked critic gradient is informative, so 1 / λ = 1 1/\lambda=1 suffices, and the adaptive EMA normalizer is preferable because the gradient magnitudes of an action chunk vary by orders of magnitude across coordinates and over training. The reference score anchors the target to the pretrained flow in both regimes. Locomotion additionally keeps the trust region Equation 16 , since with sparse rewards the critic is unreliable off the visited data and a navigation policy can otherwise drift into unseen parts of the maze. In manipulation the product tilt and chunking already keep the actor on the data, and the trust region only slows online improvement, so it is switched off. Action chunking with horizon h = 5 h=5 is part of the protocol inherited from TRQAM and is applied to all methods on the manipulation domains ( Table 3 ); it appears in Table 4 only because it coincides with the regime split.

Generating samples from this distribution can be challenging, as it is often complex and multimodal. While flow policies trained with flow matching provide a powerful framework for representing such distributions, they traditionally rely on access to training data, which is generally unavailable in online RL. To address this limitation, we propose fixed-point flow matching (FFM), a data-free procedure for training and fine-tuning flow policies in RL. FFM leverages the target flow identity to formulate the actor update as a fixed-point iteration, utilizing a flow-matching-style regression objective where the critic’s action gradients serve as regression targets. We show that the optimal policy is a fixed point of this iteration. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that FFM effectively fine-tunes pretrained flow policies in the offline-to-online setting and enables efficient and accurate training of flow policies from scratch in online RL. These results establish fixed-point flow matching as a principled approach for learning expressive flow-based policies without requiring training data. 1 Introduction Across a range of reinforcement learning (RL) formulations, the improved policy is available in closed form as a Boltzmann distribution of the current critic. In maximum entropy RL, π ⋆ ​ ( x ∣ s ) ∝ exp ⁡ ( Q ⁡ ( s , x ) / λ ) \pi^{\star}(x\mid s)\propto\exp(Q(s,x)/\lambda) is optimal for the policy improvement step of soft policy iteration ( Ziebart et al., 2008 ; Haarnoja et al., 2017 ; Haarnoja et al., 2018 ) ; in KL-regularized and behavior-constrained RL, which includes offline-to-online fine-tuning, the same expression appears tilted by a reference policy ( Peters et al., 2010 ; Abdolmaleki et al., 2018 ; Peng et al., 2019 ; Nair et al., 2020 ) . This target distribution can be complex and multimodal whenever several distinct action choices are viable, but the classical actor–critic recipe projects it onto a Gaussian due to the simplicity of the resulting optimization problem and the tractability of the policy’s log-likelihood ( Haarnoja et al., 2018 ) . Flow and diffusion models ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) remove this representational restriction and have become the policy class of choice wherever a dataset is available ( Chi et al., 2023 ; Reuss et al., 2023 ; Janner et al., 2022 ; Park et al., 2025b ) . Yet, the stable training objectives that are used to train these models are not directly usable for online RL due to a lack of samples from π ⋆ \pi^{\star} . Existing methods for training flow and diffusion models in the on-policy RL setting often require backpropagating the critic through the integrator ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Ding & Jin, 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Celik et al., 2025 ; Le et al., 2026 ) , whose memory cost grows with every integration step and quickly becomes prohibitive, or rely on importance-weighted regression ( Ding et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2025 ) , whose exponential critic weights have high variance and lead to unstable training updates. Moreover, methods for fine-tuning flow models typically use stochastic optimal control, which requires converting the flow into a diffusion model in order to use the adjoint method ( Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025 ; Li & Levine, 2026 ; Dong et al., 2026b ) . In this work we ask whether a flow policy can be trained against a Boltzmann target with the same simple regression that makes flow matching stable, but without samples from the target. Our starting point is the target flow identity : for a Boltzmann target, the velocity field that generates the noised target is, up to a rescaling of the noisy action, a conditional average of the critic’s action gradients ∇ x Q ​ ( s , x )

It replaces the data-derived regression target of flow matching by a critic-derived one, and the resulting objective, target flow matching , has the same minimizer as flow matching while reading its targets off the critic instead of a dataset. Since the objective still averages over samples of the target, we evaluate it with samples of the current policy and iterate. The resulting fixed-point flow matching (FFM) update, illustrated in Figure 1 , generates actions with the current flow, labels them with critic gradients, noises them, and regresses the velocity field onto the labels. We show that the optimal policy is a fixed point of this iteration. The whole procedure is conceptually simple, easy to implement and requires neither backpropagation through the integrator nor importance weights or conversion into a diffusion model. Contributions. • The target flow identity and target flow matching ( Section 4 ). We derive an identity that expresses the velocity field of a Boltzmann target as a conditional expectation of the gradient of its log-density, and turn it into target flow matching, an alternative training objective to flow matching that shares its population minimizer but regresses onto the gradient of the target rather than onto the displacement of the data. • Fixed-point flow matching ( Section 4 ). We propose a fixed-point iteration that evaluates the target flow matching objective with samples of the current policy instead of the optimal one, and prove that the optimal policy is a fixed point of this iteration (Theorem 3 ). • Extensions ( Section 5 ). We further introduce several extensions for flow policies: a trust-region loss in velocity space, a loss for behavior-constrained fine-tuning that reads the reference score off the pretrained flow, and correlated exploration through temporally correlated prior draws. • Two RL instantiations ( Section 5 ). We instantiate FFM for maximum entropy RL and for offline-to-online fine-tuning. We validate both across 50 50 offline-to-online tasks and 24 24 online tasks ( Section 6 ), where FFM is competitive with or better than the strongest available baselines. 2 Related work Reinforcement learning with diffusion and flow policies. Diffusion and flow models entered RL through imitation learning and offline RL, where a dataset makes their standard training objectives applicable and the critic enters through weighting, guidance, or gradients through the sampling chain ( Janner et al., 2022 ; Chi et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ; Lu et al., 2023 ; Kang et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Ding & Jin, 2024 ; Park et al., 2025b ) . In online RL there are no samples of the target policy, and existing methods differ in how the critic drives the actor update. One line backpropagates the critic value through the sampling chain ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Ding & Jin, 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) , which is memory-intensive and unstable for many integration steps. A second line uses critic-weighted regression, interpreting the denoising loss as a variational bound or as a mirror-descent step ( Ding et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2025 ) , and a third estimates policy gradients through the denoising process, typically under a trust region ( Ren et al., 2025 ; McAllister et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ; Le et al., 2026 ; Lv et al., 2026 ) . Reward fine-tuning of pretrained diffusion and flow models has been cast as policy gradient over the denoising chain ( Fan et al., 2023 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025b ) and as entropy-regularized stochastic optimal control ( Uehara et al., 2024 ; Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025 ) , with the KL divergence to the pretrained model as regularizer; Uehara et al. (2025) review the corresponding inference-time methods. The same behavior-tilted target governs offline-to-online RL with flow policies. FQL ( Park et al., 2025b ) distills the flow into a one-step policy that is trained by reparameterized critic gradients, DSRL ( Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ) keeps the flow fixed and learns a policy over its latent noise, ReinFlow and FINO ( Zhang et al., 2025a ; Shin et al., 2026b ) inject noise into the flow to obtain tractable likelihoods and exploration, and Q-Flow ( Doo et al., 2026 ) propagates terminal values to intermediate states of the flow. QAM ( Li & Levine, 2026 ) imports adjoint matching: the pretrained flow is converted into a memoryless SDE and critic gradients are transported backward along sampled trajectories by the lean adjoint ODE, and TRQAM ( Dong et al., 2026b ) stabilizes it with a path-space trust region. Concurrent work regresses velocity corrections onto critic gradients ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Ziakas et al., 2026 ) or steers a fixed flow policy at test time ( Zhou et al., 2026 ; Ruan et al., 2026 ) . FFM fine-tunes the pretrained flow directly in velocity space, requires neither SDE conversion nor adjoint simulation, and its behavior-tilted target has the KL-regularized optimum as a fixed point ( Appendix E ).
